title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World

cards.front: Name the four treatments the lesson gives for removing an excess humour.
cards.answer: Bleeding (phlebotomy) / Purging with laxatives / Sweating in hot baths / Cupping with heated jars

cards.front: Name the three types of practitioner the lesson places below the university-trained physician.
cards.answer: Barber-surgeons / Apothecaries / Wise women

cards.front: During a rare medieval dissection, why did the physician not do the cutting himself?
cards.answer: His status meant he read aloud from Galen's text while a barber-surgeon cut the body and a junior pointed at the organs.

cards.front: Why did a medieval doctor bleed a patient who had a fever?
cards.answer: A fever meant an excess of blood, linked to heat, so bleeding followed the logic of treating a hot imbalance with its opposite.

title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine

cards.front: Name the five standard surgical procedures the lesson lists for medieval barber-surgeons.
items: Cauterising wounds with a hot iron
cards.answer: Setting broken bones / Removing arrowheads / Cauterising wounds with a hot iron / Treating boils / Trepanning (drilling into the skull)

cards.front: Name the three ingredients of the medieval pain-relief mixture 'dwale'.
cards.answer: Hemlock / Opium / Lettuce juice

cards.front: How did monks in medieval monasteries keep Galen's and Hippocrates' ideas alive?
cards.answer: Monks in monasteries such as St Albans and Durham copied classical Greek and Roman medical texts by hand, preserving them for later use.

cards.front: Why couldn't medieval doctors test whether Galen's ideas were correct?
cards.answer: The 1163 Council of Tours banned clergy from cutting open bodies, so doctors had almost no way to examine bodies and check Galen's claims.

title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death

cards.front: Name the five explanations for the cause of the Black Death that the lesson gives.
items: An unfavourable conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars
cards.answer: God's punishment for sin / Miasma (bad air) / An unfavourable conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars / Blaming Jewish communities / Earthquakes releasing poisonous vapours

cards.front: Name the three areas of regulation the lesson says London tightened after the Black Death.
cards.answer: Street cleaning / Butchery rules / Burial regulations

cards.front: Why did pneumonic plague kill more people than bubonic plague, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Pneumonic plague attacked the lungs and killed almost everyone within days, while untreated bubonic plague killed only 30-60% of those infected.

cards.front: How did the Black Death contribute to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The plague caused labour shortages, and anger over the 1351 wage-fixing Statute of Labourers and a poll tax fed into the 1381 revolt.

title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen

cards.front: Name the three anatomical structures the lesson gives as examples of Vesalius correcting Galen's errors.
cards.answer: The jaw / The breastbone / The heart

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson says combined to produce Paré's salve discovery.
items: The individual (Paré recorded and published it)
cards.answer: War (many wounds to treat) / Chance (Paré ran out of oil) / The individual (Paré recorded and published it)

cards.front: Why did Paré switch from cauterising amputation wounds to using ligatures?
cards.answer: Cauterising controlled bleeding fast but often killed patients from shock, so ligatures were used instead because patients were less likely to die.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Vesalius is the textbook example of a gap between discovery and application?
cards.answer: Vesalius corrected Galen's anatomy, but British doctors had no new treatment framework, so fever patients were still treated using the four humours.

title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750

cards.front: Name the three voluntary hospitals the lesson lists as opening in 18th-century London, with their dates.
cards.answer: Westminster Hospital (1719) / Guy's (1724) / The London (1740)

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson credits to Sydenham's clinical approach.
items: Describing gout from his own experience
Using cinchona bark for malarial fevers
cards.answer: Distinguishing scarlet fever from measles / Describing gout from his own experience / Using cinchona bark for malarial fevers

cards.front: How did Harvey's discovery of circulation undermine bleeding as a treatment?
cards.answer: If blood circulates continuously round the body, removing pints of it through bleeding weakens the patient rather than restoring any balance.

cards.front: How did the same printing technology that spread Harvey's ideas also enable quackery?
cards.answer: The same cheap printing and newspapers that spread scientific findings like Harvey's also let quack doctors advertise patent remedies to a wide public.

title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why vaccination was different from inoculation.
items: Could not spread smallpox to others
cards.answer: Much safer (cowpox rarely killed) / Could not spread smallpox to others / Cheaper to produce

cards.front: Name the three sources of opposition to vaccination described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Inoculators (losing business) / Clergy (called it against God's plan) / Ordinary people (fear of something new)

cards.front: Why was Jenner's vaccination method vulnerable to opposition despite working?
cards.answer: Jenner could not explain why vaccination worked because he had no theory of immunity or germ theory, which let opponents attack it.

cards.front: Why does the lesson call vaccination the first major medical intervention where government took a serious role?
cards.answer: Parliament gave Jenner large cash grants and later passed laws making vaccination compulsory, marking government's first serious financial and legal role in medicine.

title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution

cards.front: Name the three patent remedies the lesson gives as examples still sold in the market during the age of germ theory.
cards.answer: Beecham's Pills / Carter's Little Liver Pills / Bovril (marketed as a tonic)

cards.front: Name the three traditional remedies doctors kept prescribing alongside new hygiene advice, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Cod liver oil / Beef tea / Mustard plasters

cards.front: Why was miasma theory able to produce useful public health action even though it was wrong?
cards.answer: Miasma theory logically linked bad smells to danger, so removing foul smells through ventilation, street cleaning and lime in graveyards often reduced disease anyway.

cards.front: How did French-German rivalry speed up the pace of germ theory discoveries?
cards.answer: Each new discovery by one country's scientist provoked a rival response from the other, and governments funded laboratories partly to outcompete each other.

title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

cards.front: Name the three early anaesthetics the lesson lists, with who introduced each.
cards.answer: Nitrous oxide (Davy, 1799) / Ether (Morton, 1846) / Chloroform (Simpson, 1847)

cards.front: Name the four practices of aseptic surgery the lesson describes.
items: Wearing surgical gowns and face masks
cards.answer: Sterilising instruments in steam autoclaves / Wearing surgical gowns and face masks / Scrubbing hands before operating / Using rubber gloves

cards.front: Why did the 'Black Period' see more surgical deaths after anaesthetics arrived?
cards.answer: Anaesthetics let surgeons operate for longer and more often, but filthy theatres and unsterilised instruments meant infection killed far more patients than before.

cards.front: How did Lister's reading of Pasteur's germ theory lead him to try carbolic acid on wounds?
cards.answer: Lister reasoned that if germs in the air caused decay, they must also cause wound infection, so he tried carbolic acid, already used to deodorise sewage.

title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts

cards.front: Name the four major cholera epidemics the lesson lists for 19th-century Britain, by date.
Name the three other Acts the lesson says the same Parliament passed alongside the 1875 Public Health Act.
items: Sale of Food and Drugs Act
cards.answer: Artisans' Dwellings Act (slum clearance) / Sale of Food and Drugs Act / Rivers Pollution Prevention Act

cards.front: Why did cholera survive in some parts of London in 1866 but not others, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Bazalgette's new sewer system was working in the West End and central London, so cholera killed people mainly in districts that were still unsewered.

cards.front: How did the 1867 Reform Act help bring about the 1875 Public Health Act?
cards.answer: The 1867 Reform Act gave working-class men in towns the vote, so MPs now needed the support of slum-dwelling voters.

title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing

cards.front: Name the six elements of nursing knowledge that Notes on Nursing set out, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Observation / Hygiene / Ventilation / Diet / Quiet / Light

cards.front: Name the three features of the pavilion plan design that the lesson describes.
items: Windows on both sides for cross-ventilation
cards.answer: Windows on both sides for cross-ventilation / Separate buildings for different diseases / High ceilings

cards.front: Why did mortality at Scutari fall so sharply between 1854 and spring 1855?
cards.answer: The government's Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers in March 1855, and this combined with Nightingale's regime of cleanliness cut the death rate sharply.

cards.front: Why did Nightingale's polar-area chart succeed in convincing Parliament, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Nightingale's statistics gave hospital reform an evidence base of hard data rather than anecdote, which critics found much harder to dismiss.

title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914

cards.front: Name the three reforms for children the lesson lists under the Liberal reforms.
cards.answer: Free School Meals (1906) / School Medical Inspections (1907) / The Children Act, the 'Children's Charter' (1908)

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says opposed the Liberal welfare reforms.
items: Conservatives in the House of Lords
cards.answer: The British Medical Association / Conservatives in the House of Lords / Friendly societies / The Labour Party

cards.front: Why did the Boer War turn welfare into a political priority, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Rejecting 40% of recruits as unfit turned welfare from a moral question into a national-security question about fielding an effective army.

cards.front: Why did the Liberals only assemble their welfare reform programme after winning power in 1906, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The Liberals had no 1906 manifesto for welfare; the programme was built in office to head off Labour and respond to Booth, Rowntree and the Boer War.

title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars

cards.front: Name the three classes of antibiotic the lesson lists as multiplying after penicillin.
cards.answer: Streptomycin (1944, for tuberculosis) / Tetracyclines / Cephalosporins

cards.front: Name the four modern health challenges the lesson says earlier eras barely recognised.
items: Dementia and cancer from an ageing population
cards.answer: HIV/AIDS (from the 1980s) / Dementia and cancer from an ageing population / Mental health conditions / Lifestyle illnesses (diet, smoking, alcohol)

cards.front: Why couldn't Britain turn Fleming's 1928 discovery into a usable medicine on its own?
cards.answer: Fleming could not purify penicillin in useful quantities, and wartime Britain lacked the industrial capacity to mass-produce it once Florey and Chain had purified it.

cards.front: How did MRSA emerge as a threat, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: MRSA emerged in the 1960s as bacteria evolved resistance to antibiotics that had been over-prescribed since the 1940s.

title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS

cards.front: Name the five giants named in the Beveridge Report.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Name the three preconditions the Beveridge Report assumed for its welfare scheme to work.
cards.answer: Family allowances for children / A free national health service / Full employment

cards.front: Why did Bevan compromise with the BMA over consultants' private practice and GP contracts?
cards.answer: Bevan let consultants keep private patients on NHS pay-beds and made GPs self-employed contractors, without which doctors would have blocked the NHS launch.

cards.front: How did wartime evacuation change middle-class attitudes to welfare, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Evacuation exposed middle-class hosts to the poverty, hunger and poor health of city children for the first time, building support for welfare reform.

title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of government dominating twentieth-century medicine.
cards.answer: 1875 Public Health Act (compulsory) / Liberal reforms 1906-11 / NHS 1948

cards.front: Name the four wars the lesson lists as accelerating medical change.
items: World War One (transfusion, plastic surgery, X-rays)
cards.answer: Crimean War (Nightingale) / Boer War (Liberal reforms) / World War One (transfusion, plastic surgery, X-rays) / World War Two (penicillin, NHS preconditions)

cards.front: How did government's role in fighting disease change between 1348 and 1875, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Government moved from almost no action in 1348, through an ignored voluntary 1848 law, to a compulsory and comprehensive Act in 1875.

cards.front: Why does the lesson group the 1853 Vaccination Act and the 1948 NHS together as contested change?
cards.answer: Both faced organised opposition - anti-vaccination resistance to the 1853 Act and the British Medical Association's attack on the 1948 NHS.
